title: Palm Sunday
hookLine: the palms and the long passion read with the whole congregation

cards: Ushers stand at the door handing out strips of palm, and within a minute some kid is sword fighting with one, or folding it into a cross. The service begins outside, or at the back, with a procession and singing.
Branches wave. It feels like a parade. Then, not long after, the same congregation, holding the same palms, will read aloud a line nobody wants to say.
This is a Sunday that turns around in the middle.

teach.b: First, the entry. Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a donkey, a king's entrance done humbly, as the prophet Zechariah had pictured.

People throw their cloaks and branches on the road and shout, in Matthew's account in the Douay-Rheims: "Hosanna to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord: Hosanna in the highest."
Hosanna is Hebrew, from Psalm 118: save, please. A cry for rescue that had become a shout of welcome. The palms are blessed and the people process, re-enacting it.
Then the Mass begins, and the gospel is the Passion, the whole account of his arrest, trial and death, from Matthew, Mark or Luke depending on the year.
It's long, and it may be read in parts: a reader narrates, the priest takes the words of Jesus, and the congregation reads the crowd.
So the same voices that sang hosanna at the door find themselves saying, together, crucify him. That's deliberate. The Church isn't pointing at a crowd long ago and saying, look what they did.
It's handing the line to everyone in the pews. Catholic teaching is clear that the blame for his death falls on all sinners, not on any one people.
People take the palms home and tuck them behind a crucifix or a picture, and next year, as Ash Wednesday's lesson told, palms like these become the ashes.
This week behind us: forty days, upon this rock, christ in every eye, the silent saint, be it done, halfway, rejoice. Now the week everything has pointed toward.

how: On Palm Sunday of the Passion of the Lord, Catholics receive blessed palms, process into church, and hear the Passion read, sometimes in parts with the congregation reading the crowd; some keep the palms at home until next year's Ash Wednesday.

o: the Sunday after Easter, with palms for joy
the feast of Jesus's baptism, with branches

s: it's Hebrew from Psalm 118: save, please.
Catholic teaching blames one people for Jesus's death
it teaches that the blame falls on all sinners, which is why the congregation reads the crowd.
in Matthew, the crowd spreads branches and cloaks on the road
and cries hosanna to the son of David.

games.q: you're in the pew, palm in hand. the Passion is being read in parts, and the crowd's line comes up. it's yours. what do you say?
o: skip it; it's not my line.
games.why: the congregation reads the crowd: crucify him. the same voices that sang hosanna at the door. the Church hands the line to everyone.

practice: If you have a palm from church, find a place for it, behind a crucifix, over a door, tucked into a picture frame; if not, set any green leaf or small branch where you'll see it this week.
Sit with it and think how quickly cheering can turn, in a crowd, in a friendship, in yourself. If you pray, say the old cry, hosanna, save, please; if not, simply hold the leaf and the week ahead.

wordCard.voice: Palm Sunday. The Sunday before Easter: palms and a procession, then the Passion read aloud, with the congregation as the crowd. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: save, please, from Psalm 118:25; the root of hosanna.

carryVoice: Your line: hosanna, then crucify. The same mouths, the same week. Day six hundred fifty-eight, done.
